newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil vulnerabilities budget, c/a deficits - Malan.
newsitem.headline: Brazil vulnerabilities budget, c/a deficits - Malan.

text.p: Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan said in a newspaper interview that the main vulnerabilities of the government's economic policy were deficits in the budget and the balance of payments' current account.

In an interview published Monday in the Gazeta Mercantil, he said that the public sector fiscal accounts were improving, but that the trend toward an increase in the current account deficit had to inspire caution.

He said the nominal public sector deficit fell to 5.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the first two months of this year. This compares with a nominal deficit of 7.5 percent of GDP in 1995 and a deficit of 6.05 percent of GDP in 1996, Malan said.
"There are people who believe this is not fast enough, but economics and politics interact," he said. "We have no dictatorship here."

He said the main cause for the current account deficit was a disequilibrium between savings and investments, and not Brazil's growing trade gap, which accounted for only 20 percent of the current account deficit.
"The fundamental cure for the current account deficit is to increase personal savings and reduce the lack of public sector saving," Malan said.
He said this year's current account deficit, which would be "a little higher" than last year's 3.3 percent of GDP, was not very high according to international standards.
It was being financed with "capital of better quality," especially as the influx of direct investments increased, Malan said.
Direct investment in Brazil amounted to $11 billion in the 12 months to the end of March, up from $9.4 billion in 1996, Malan said.

He said a drastic readjustment of Brazil's real currency exchange rate was not justified in order to improve the country's trade performance, adding that claims of the real being overvalued by 46, 30 or 20 percent were exaggerated.
"Serious people are quoting figures well below that," Malan said. "And I'm saying that something well below that can be adjusted gradually."
In answer to a question, Malan denied the government's economic policy would increasingly be dictated by the election calendar as the re-election of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso approached.
"We shall do what needs to be done," he said.
((--Simona de Logu, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 507 4151))
